messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-five when a man with a knife took his wallet on a darkened street corner three blocks from his apartment. The mugging itself lasted perhaps ninety seconds—a figure emerging from shadow, the blade catching streetlight, a voice that was almost conversational in its demand. What Marcus remembered most vividly, what played back in his mind with the clarity of a photograph he could not look away from, was the moment the man's hand closed around his neck. The pressure was sudden and absolute. The attacker's face—thin, weathered, eyes that seemed to contain nothing—filled Marcus's entire visual field. Then the shove that sent him sprawling, the sound of retreating footsteps, the burning in his throat and the sharp, radiating pain in his neck where the man's fingers had dug in. When Marcus tried to stand, his legs would not obey him. He sat on the cold pavement for what felt like hours but was probably minutes, touching his neck, half-convinced he was bleeding.

He was not bleeding. The police came. They asked questions in voices that were patient but clinical, and Marcus answered them, though he could not quite hear himself speaking. In the weeks that followed, the memory did not fade. Instead, it crystallized. Whenever something triggered the recollection—a shout in the street, a sudden sound, the sight of a police uniform—the memory would return with such photographic intensity that Marcus would feel the pressure on his neck all over again, would smell the man's clothes, would see that empty face. His body would respond as if the threat were happening in the present moment. The flashbacks came without warning. Once, a student in his special education classroom raised his voice in frustration, and Marcus felt his breath catch, felt his hands move instinctively to his throat. He had to excuse himself, locking himself in the staff bathroom for twenty minutes while his heart hammered against his ribs.

The neck pain itself—a dull, persistent ache that radiated from where the man's fingers had pressed—became another trigger. When he felt it, the memory surfaced. When the memory surfaced, the pain seemed to intensify, as if his body were confirming the danger all over again. Marcus could not relax, not even when he was alone in his apartment with the doors locked and the lights on. His mind would not accept that he was safe. He began to scan every room he entered, noting exits, calculating distances, assessing threat. In his classroom, he positioned himself near the door. In restaurants, he sat facing the entrance. In the grocery store, his eyes moved constantly from aisle to aisle, cataloging people, movements, anything that might be a threat.

What made this worse—what made the hypervigilance feel not like paranoia but like necessity—was the conviction that had settled into his bones: that he was inadequate, that someone else would have handled the situation differently. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation in the first place. He had been careless, walking that route at that hour, not paying attention. He was weak, and the memory of his own helplessness—the way his body had failed him, the way he had sat on the pavement unable to move—fed a rage that consumed him when he recalled the event. But alongside the rage came guilt. He should have fought back. He should have been stronger. He should have been better. These beliefs made the threat feel permanent and internal. He was not just in danger from the world; he was inadequate to meet it. This sense of his own insufficiency meant he could never truly relax, never believe himself safe, because the danger was partly him. His hypervigilance was not irrational; it was the only rational response to living with someone fundamentally unprepared for the world.

By month four, Marcus had stopped going out except for work and essential errands. He avoided the neighborhood where the mugging occurred, then avoided the adjacent neighborhoods, then found reasons not to travel anywhere unfamiliar. His colleagues noticed he was quieter, more withdrawn. He had turned down the departmental happy hour three times. When a police officer visited the school for a safety presentation, Marcus felt his chest tighten the moment the man entered the building, and he spent the entire assembly staring at his hands. The threat was constant now—not episodic, but woven into the texture of his daily life. It was this relentless exhaustion, this sense that he would never be safe and never be adequate to the task of keeping himself safe, that finally brought him to a therapist's office on a gray November afternoon. He sat in the waiting room, scanning the exits, and wondered if talking about it would make the photographs in his mind finally fade, or whether he was simply broken in a way that could not be repaired.
